# k0rdent_vpc_security_groups (Resource)

The security groups attached to a VPC, in the order the fabric applies them.

A VPC is materialized by a cluster or instance group and has no lifecycle of its own, so this binding is the only part of one that Terraform can write. It is a whole-list replace: the groups named here are attached, and any attached before and absent now are detached.

**Destroying this resource does not leave the VPC unfiltered.** It reinstates the VPC's platform-managed DEFAULT group, which permits traffic between the VPC's own subnet prefixes and permits all egress. A VPC always carries at least one group. A replacement does the same to the old VPC, because it destroys the old binding. The plan warns about a destroy, and about a replacement that a change to `vpc`, `region` or `project` causes. It can't warn about one forced by `-replace` or `replace_triggered_by`, because Terraform decides those without asking the provider.

A destroy only clears the binding this resource holds. It reads the VPC first, and if the VPC holds anything but the list this resource last read, in the same order, or holds a list another instance of this resource wrote earlier in the same apply, it leaves the VPC as it is, drops the resource from state and warns. That's what makes `create_before_destroy` safe on the same VPC: the new binding is written first, and the old one's destroy finds it and leaves it, even when it names the same groups, as `-replace` does. It also means a destroy doesn't undo a binding that another configuration or the console set since the last refresh. Writes to the same VPC from this apply wait for the destroy's read and write to finish. A change from anywhere else that lands between them is still overwritten, because the platform has no conditional write for a binding.

These groups are applied *after* the owning cluster or instance group's own groups, so an interface inside this VPC filters on the owner's groups first. A group attached to both is applied once, at the owner's position. Writing here re-renders the owner's network bundles, which is why the owner goes transitional for a moment.

Only a VPC on the `nico` fabric backend can carry security groups. Read `backend` from the `k0rdent_vpc` data source first.

Requires `region` and `project` on the provider.

**What replaces it.** Changing `project`, `region` or `vpc` cannot be done in place and replaces the binding. Everything else changes in place.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# An instance group has its own VPC. Take it from the group, not a data
# source, so a change to the group doesn't replace this binding.
resource "k0rdent_vpc_security_groups" "hosts" {
  vpc = k0rdent_instance_group.hosts.vpc

  security_groups = [
    k0rdent_security_group.office_access.id,
  ]
}
```

```terraform
# Order matters: groups apply in list order and the first matching rule wins.
resource "k0rdent_vpc_security_groups" "training" {
  vpc = local.training_vpc

  security_groups = [
    k0rdent_security_group.office_access.id,
    k0rdent_security_group.baseline.id,
  ]
}

# Destroying this puts back the VPC's default group, which allows traffic
# inside the VPC and all egress. `attached` shows what's bound.
output "actually_attached" {
  value = k0rdent_vpc_security_groups.training.attached
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `security_groups` (List of String) Ids of the groups to attach, in the order the fabric should apply them. Order is significant: it reaches the fabric as written, and rule evaluation is first-match.

An empty list is accepted and means *reinstate the default group*, not *attach nothing*. **Constraints:** List must contain at most 16 elements. Each security group id must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, not ending with a hyphen, and at most 63 characters long.
- `vpc` (String) Id of the VPC to bind. This is also the id this resource is imported by, because a VPC has exactly one binding. **Forces replacement**. **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL.

### Optional

- `project` (String) Project this resource belongs to. Defaults to the provider's `project`. It's part of the resource's API path, so a resource can't move between projects. **Forces replacement**. **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL.
- `region` (String) Region this resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `region`. It's part of the resource's API path, so a resource can't move between regions. **Forces replacement**. **Constraints:** Must be lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen (`[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?`), because it becomes a segment of a request URL.
- `timeouts` (Block, Optional) How long each operation may take before it fails. Each operation left out defaults to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--timeouts))

### Read-Only

- `attached` (List of String) What the platform reports as attached after the write. This differs from `security_groups` when the list sent was empty, because the default group is then reported here explicitly.
- `state` (String) The VPC's lifecycle state as last read. `updating` means the binding has been accepted and is still being rendered onto the owner's network bundles, so `attached` is what the platform will converge on rather than necessarily what the fabric enforces yet.

<a id="nestedblock--timeouts"></a>
### Nested Schema for `timeouts`

Optional:

- `create` (String) Bounds the whole create, including the wait until the platform reports it ready. Left out, it defaults to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.
- `delete` (String) Bounds the whole destroy, including the wait until the platform reports it gone. Left out, it defaults to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.
- `update` (String) Bounds the whole update, including the wait until the platform settles. Left out, it defaults to the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. **Constraints:** Must be a positive duration of hours, minutes or seconds, such as `45m`, `2h` or `1h30m`.

## Timeouts

The `timeouts` block sets how long each operation may take before it fails:

- `create` (default `2h`). Bounds the whole create, including the wait until the platform reports it ready.
- `update` (default `2h`). Bounds the whole update, including the wait until the platform settles.
- `delete` (default `2h`). Bounds the whole destroy, including the wait until the platform reports it gone.

Each default is the provider's `operation_timeout`, which is `2h` unless the provider block or `K0RDENT_OPERATION_TIMEOUT` sets it. An operation the block leaves out takes that value, so raising `operation_timeout` raises all of them at once. A value of zero or less is refused at plan time rather than read as no limit.

A wait that runs out, or a run that is interrupted, stops nothing on the platform. A create that stops waiting fails, and Terraform taints the object: run `terraform untaint` on it and then `terraform apply`, which waits for the same object. A delete that stops waiting fails and stays in state, and the next `terraform destroy` waits for the same delete without sending another.

```terraform
resource "k0rdent_vpc_security_groups" "example" {
  # ...

  timeouts {
    create = "45m"
    update = "45m"
    delete = "45m"
  }
}
```

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

In Terraform v1.12.0 and later, the [`import` block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import) can be used with the `identity` attribute, for example:

```terraform
# The same address with each part named. Leave out region and project to
# use the provider's.
import {
  to = k0rdent_vpc_security_groups.example
  identity = {
    region  = "us-texas-1"
    project = "cp-production"
    vpc     = "vpc-training"
  }
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
### Identity Schema

#### Required

- `vpc` (String) Id of the VPC, which is what names this resource.

#### Optional

- `project` (String) Project the resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `project` on import.
- `region` (String) Region the resource lives in. Defaults to the provider's `region` on import.

In Terraform v1.5.0 and later, the [`import` block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import) can be used with the `id` attribute, for example:

```terraform
# Takes every id form `terraform import` does. The VPC's id is the address.
# The first command below gives that id, the second names the scope too.
#
# A VPC with only its default group imports as security_groups = [].
import {
  to = k0rdent_vpc_security_groups.example
  id = "us-texas-1/cp-production/vpc-training"
}
```

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
terraform import k0rdent_vpc_security_groups.example vpc-training

terraform import k0rdent_vpc_security_groups.example us-texas-1/cp-production/vpc-training
```
